title: Neck Pain: Common Causes, What Helps and When to See a Doctor
metaDescription: Most neck pain settles within a few weeks. Learn the common causes, simple self-care, how pain is treated and the warning signs that need a doctor.
intro: Most neck pain is short-lived and settles within a few weeks. Gentle movement, heat or cold and common pain medicines are usually enough. Common causes are sleeping awkwardly, long hours at a desk, muscle strain and injury. See a doctor if the pain lasts beyond a few weeks, if medicines do not help, or if you have tingling, weakness or other warning signs. This page explains the causes and our usual approach to treatment.

sections.heading: What usually causes neck pain?
sections.body: The NHS lists waking up with the neck stuck in an awkward position, poor posture such as long hours of desk sitting, a pinched nerve, and injury such as whiplash from a road accident or a fall. Versus Arthritis adds that holding the neck in one position for too long is the usual reason, and that age-related wear of the discs and joints in the neck can contribute. Often there is no clear trigger at all. Neck problems can also cause pain in the upper back, shoulders or arms.

sections.heading: How long does neck pain last?
sections.body: Most neck pain only lasts a few weeks, according to the NHS. Orthopaedic specialists in the United States describe it as a problem that, for many people, disappears with time. Tests are usually not needed. An X-ray, blood test or MRI is used only occasionally, to rule out other causes. Most people can return to work within two to three days.

sections.heading: What can I do at home?
sections.body: Staying gently active usually helps more than resting. Rest for a day or two if you need to, then keep the neck moving.
bullets: Use heat or cold. The NHS suggests frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel for 5 minutes, or a wrapped hot water bottle for 20 minutes, a few times a day.
Use a low, firm pillow and keep your head level with the rest of your body when you sleep.
Avoid sleeping on your front or twisting your neck in bed.
Sit upright and avoid holding one neck position for long periods.
Do not wear a neck collar unless a doctor advises it, because keeping the neck moving is preferred.

sections.heading: Which medicines help neck pain?
sections.body: Our usual approach is to start with medicines to settle the pain. The NHS suggests paracetamol, ibuprofen, or ibuprofen gel rubbed on the neck. Versus Arthritis advises anti-inflammatory tablets such as ibuprofen for about 5 to 10 days only. These tablets are not suitable for everyone, for example people with asthma, stomach ulcers or heart problems, or those taking warfarin. Check with a pharmacist or doctor first. If pain does not settle, stronger medicines are an option.

sections.heading: What if the pain does not settle?
sections.body: Once pain eases, exercises to stretch and strengthen the neck and shoulders work best, and we build them up gradually. If pain is still limiting you, physiotherapy treatments such as ultrasound, short-wave or TENS (a small electrical stimulation device) may be tried, for pain relief only. The evidence for these is modest, and NICE guidance on low back pain advises against offering TENS and ultrasound. An injection is considered only for selected patients, to ease pain. Surgery is the last step, only if appropriate. The decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor about neck pain?
sections.body: The NHS advises seeing a doctor if pain has not improved after a few weeks, if paracetamol or ibuprofen have not helped, or if you have pins and needles or a cold arm. Get care at once after a serious injury such as a road accident or fall, and keep the person still. These signs also need prompt assessment:
bullets: Pain, numbness, tingling or weakness spreading into the arms or legs
Trouble with fine tasks such as buttoning clothes or holding things
Fever, feeling generally unwell, or unexplained weight loss
Pain that is worse at night or does not ease with rest
Loss of control of urine or stools, or numbness around the genitals or back passage

faqs.a: Usually not. Most neck pain is from strained muscles and settles in a few weeks. Rarely it signals a more serious problem, which is why the warning signs above matter.

faqs.q: Should I use heat or cold?
faqs.a: Either can be used. Heat often soothes muscle spasm, and cold may help after a strain. Wrap the pack in a cloth and use it for a short time.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI for neck pain?
faqs.a: Usually not. Scans are used occasionally to rule out other causes, for example when there is arm weakness or numbness, or when pain does not settle.
Yes. Versus Arthritis lists stress among the things that can contribute. Gentle exercise, good sleep and regular breaks from screens can help.

faqs.q: Is it safe to exercise with neck pain?
faqs.a: Gentle neck movement is advised. Stop and get advice if exercise brings on sharp pain, tingling or weakness.

faqs.q: Can I take painkillers every day?
faqs.a: Tablets are meant for short courses of about 5 to 10 days. If you need them for longer, see a doctor so the cause can be looked at.

If pain is limiting your daily activities or sleep, Dr. Niranjan Ghag, orthopaedic surgeon in Thane West, can examine you and explain your options at a consultation; the decision about treatment, including whether you need surgery at all, stays with you. Seek prompt help after a serious injury, or if neck pain comes with weakness or numbness in the arms or legs, fever, unexplained weight loss, pain at night, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
